pos: n. (want of self-restraint, especially in the appetites; the AV has incontinency and incontinent)
etymology: Latin incontinentia, from in-, not, and continere, to hold together — a man who cannot hold himself. The AV's incontinent at 2 Timothy 3:3 means without self-control, not the modern medical sense.
biblical_def: Incontinence is want of self-restraint. Paul uses it of the married withholding from one another: come together again, “that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency” (1Co 7:5), and gives the practical counsel, “if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn” (1Co 7:9). He lists incontinent among the marks of the last days: men shall be “false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good” (2Ti 3:3). The opposite is fruit: “meekness, temperance: against such there is no law” (Gal 5:23). And Proverbs gives the image: “He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls” (Pro 25:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines incontinence as want of restraint of the passions or appetites; and incontinent as not restraining the passions or appetites, unchaste.
webster_full: INCONTINENCE, INCONTINENCY, n. Want of restraint of the passions or appetites; free or uncontrolled indulgence of the passions.
2. Want of restraint of the sexual appetite; free or illegal indulgence of lust; lewdness.
INCONTINENT, a. Not restraining the passions or appetites, particularly the sexual appetite; indulging lust without restraint or in violation of law; unchaste; lewd.
scriptures: Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.
But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.
Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,
Gal 5:23
Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.
He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
corruption_summary: Self-control is treated as the sum of holiness, and Galatians lists it last among nine fruits of the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 25:28 gives the image that explains why incontinence is so destructive and it is architectural rather than moral. A man with no rule over his own spirit is a city broken down and without walls — not a wicked city, an undefended one. The damage comes from whatever happens to arrive next, because nothing is keeping anything out. That is why the fault touches everything: temper, money, speech, appetite and time all run through the same breach, and a man who cannot govern one usually cannot govern the others.

The Reformed correction to a merely moralistic account is in Galatians 5:23, where temperance appears as the last of nine fruits of the Spirit. It grows; it is not manufactured. This matters pastorally, because self-control pursued directly by willpower produces either a Pharisee or a despairing man, and often the same man in sequence. What Scripture prescribes is not more clenching but a life fed at the root — walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh — with the restraint following as fruit follows sap.

First Corinthians 7 is startlingly practical and the church has often been embarrassed by it. Paul tells married couples not to defraud one another except by consent for a time, and to come together again that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency — treating the marriage bed as, among other things, a defence. Verse 9 is equally plain: if they cannot contain, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn. That is counsel given to real people about a real appetite, and it assumes neither that the appetite is shameful nor that it is uncontrollable, which is the balance most advice on the subject loses.
roots_summary: Greek akrasia (G192), incontinency, want of self-control; akrates (G193), incontinent, powerless over oneself; egkrateia (G1466), temperance, self-mastery; egkrateuomai (G1467), to contain oneself.
roots_lines: Greek akrasia (G192) — incontinency; 1 Corinthians 7:5, Matthew 23:25 — both occurrences.
Greek akrates (G193) — without self-control, incontinent; 2 Timothy 3:3 only.
Greek egkrateia (G1466) — temperance, self-mastery; Galatians 5:23, Acts 24:25, 2 Peter 1:6.
usage: “A city that is broken down, and without walls” — undefended, not wicked.
“Meekness, temperance” — last of nine fruits, and it grows.
“If they cannot contain, let them marry” — counsel to real people.

pos: n. (inherent baseness; the shamefulness of an act considered in itself)
etymology: Latin turpitudo, from turpis, foul, base. The word describes the quality of a deed rather than its consequences — what it is, apart from who was harmed.
biblical_def: Turpitude is baseness in the act itself. Paul reaches the edge of what he will describe: “it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret” (Eph 5:12), having already named the exchange of the natural use for that which is against nature (Rom 1:26). Ezekiel is commissioned to make it visible: “cause Jerusalem to know her abominations” (Eze 16:2). Peter describes a settled condition: “having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin” (2Pe 2:14). And Jude's image is of something that surfaces on its own: “raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame” (Jud 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines turpitude as inherent baseness or vileness of principle or actions; shameful wickedness; and everything contrary to justice, honesty, modesty or decency.
webster_full: TURPITUDE, n. Inherent baseness or vileness of principle or actions; shameful wickedness; depravity.
Every thing contrary to justice, honesty, modesty or decency, is a moral turpitude.
scriptures: Eph 5:12
For it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret.
Rom 1:26
For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature:
Eze 16:2
Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations,
Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin; beguiling unstable souls: an heart they have exercised with covetous practices; cursed children:
Jud 1:13
Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.
corruption_summary: Sin is measured only by the harm it causes, and Scripture also weighs what an act is in itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is to measure a deed entirely by its consequences: if no one was harmed, no wrong was done. Scripture does not reason that way. Ephesians 5:12 speaks of things done in secret, where by definition no third party is injured, and calls it a shame even to mention them. The category of turpitude exists because acts have a moral quality independent of their outcomes — they are fitting or unfitting to what a human being is — and a conscience trained only on harm will eventually be unable to see anything wrong in the private.

The preaching difficulty is real and Paul names it. He will not describe what he is condemning, and neither should a pulpit; a sermon that gives the details has done the congregation an injury under cover of warning them. Yet Ezekiel is commanded to cause Jerusalem to know her abominations, and does so in some of the most explicit chapters in the Bible. The two are not in conflict: Ezekiel is naming a nation's sin to that nation, Paul is restraining discussion of what outsiders do in the dark, and the difference is who is being addressed and to what end.

Second Peter 2:14 supplies the trajectory and it is the reason turpitude is worth a doctrine rather than a shudder: eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin. The inability arrives after the appetite has been fed long enough, and the man does not choose the day on which the capacity to stop leaves him. Jude adds that such shame surfaces of itself, as the sea foams out what is in it. Which is the only comfort available here: nothing stays secret, and the God who sees it now is the God who offers cleansing now.
roots_summary: Greek aischron (G150), shameful; atimia (G819), vileness, dishonour; aselgeia (G766), lasciviousness; Hebrew toebah (H8441), abomination.
roots_lines: Greek aischron (G150) — shameful, base; Ephesians 5:12, 1 Corinthians 11:6, 14:35, Titus 1:11.
Greek pathe atimias (G819) — vile affections; Romans 1:26.
Hebrew toebah (H8441) — abomination; Ezekiel 16:2, 16:22, 8:6, Leviticus 18:22.
usage: “A shame even to speak of those things… in secret” — where no third party is harmed.
“That cannot cease from sin” — and he did not choose the day.
“Foaming out their own shame” — it surfaces of itself.

pos: adj. (grossly criminal; villainous beyond the common measure)
etymology: Latin flagitiosus, from flagitium, a shameful act — related to flagitare, to demand hotly, and so originally the deed a hot passion demands.
biblical_def: A flagitious act is criminality of a kind that shocks even a corrupt society. God says of Sodom, “because their sin is very grievous” (Gen 18:20). Ezekiel is shown worse and worse: “turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations” (Eze 8:6). Jeremiah reports a national condition: “A wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land” (Jer 5:30). Paul finds in the church at Corinth “such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles” (1Co 5:1). And the outrage at Gibeah draws the strongest sentence in Judges: “there was no such deed done nor seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt unto this day” (Jdg 19:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines flagitious as deeply criminal; grossly wicked; villainous; atrocious; and, of a person, guilty of enormous crimes.
webster_full: FLAGITIOUS, a. Deeply criminal; grossly wicked; villainous; atrocious; scandalous; as a flagitious action or crime.
2. Guilty of enormous crimes; corrupt; wicked; as a flagitious person.
3. Very wicked; corrupt; abandoned; as flagitious times.
scriptures: And the LORD said, Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous;
Eze 8:6

He said furthermore unto me, Son of man, seest thou what they do? even the great abominations that the house of Israel committeth here, that I should go far off from my sanctuary? but turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations.
Jer 5:30
A wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land;
It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife.

And it was so, that all that saw it said, There was no such deed done nor seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt unto this day: consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds.
corruption_summary: The church expects gross wickedness outside its walls, and Paul's example is a case inside a congregation that was proud of itself.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 5:1 is the passage that should stop any congregation from locating this word entirely outside itself. There is fornication among you, Paul writes, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles — the pagans of Corinth, a city whose morals were a byword in the ancient world, would have been shocked. And the next clause is worse: and ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned. The congregation was proud. Not of the sin, but of a tolerance that felt like maturity, and Paul's charge is that they had not grieved.

Judges 19 is the darkest chapter in the Old Testament and the narrator does not editorialise; he lets the deed stand and records Israel's reaction: consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds. The book's refrain explains how a nation arrives there — in those days there was no king in Israel, every man did that which was right in his own eyes — and the sequence matters. Flagitious acts appear at the end of a process in which each man became his own standard, and they appear among the covenant people.

The reason to keep the category at all is that a church without it will handle grave sin as though it were ordinary, and Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 5 is severe precisely because the case was. Yet the same apostle, writing to the same church later, orders the restoration of a disciplined man lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Both letters are in the canon. A church that can do only the severity or only the restoration has half of what was given it, and the half it has will eventually harm someone.
roots_summary: Hebrew rabbah meod (H7227), very grievous; shaarurah (H8186), a horrible thing; nebalah (H5039), folly, an outrage; Greek porneia (G4202), fornication.
roots_lines: Hebrew chatathah kabedah meod (H3515) — their sin is very grievous; Genesis 18:20.
Hebrew nebalah (H5039) — folly, an outrage; Judges 19:23–24, 20:6, Genesis 34:7, 2 Samuel 13:12.
Greek porneia (G4202) — fornication; 1 Corinthians 5:1, 6:13, 6:18, Galatians 5:19.
usage: “Not so much as named among the Gentiles” — and it was in the church.
“Ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned” — the congregation was proud.
“Consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds” — and the narrator says no more.

pos: n. (prudent economy; a good husbandry of what one has been given)
etymology: Latin frugalitas, from frux, fruit or produce — a frugal man is a fruitful one, who gets increase out of what he has. The root is agricultural, not miserly.
biblical_def: Frugality is good husbandry. The Lord practises it after feeding five thousand from a boy's lunch: “Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost” (John 6:12) — abundance and thrift in the same miracle. Proverbs contrasts the two habits: “There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up” (Pro 21:20), and describes accumulation by increments: “he that gathereth by labour shall increase” (Pro 13:11). The ant is set as a teacher: she “provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest” (Pro 6:8). And the floor of contentment is set low: “having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines frugality as prudent economy; good husbandry or housewifery; a sparing use or appropriation of money or commodities; and notes that frugality is not parsimony.
webster_full: FRUGALITY, n. Prudent economy; good husbandry or housewifery; a sparing use or appropriation of money or commodities; a judicious use of any thing to be expended or employed.
Without frugality none can be rich, and with it few would be poor.
2. A prudent and sparing use or appropriation of any thing; as frugality of praise.
FRUGAL, a. Economical in the use or appropriation of money, goods or provisions of any kind; saving unnecessary expense.
scriptures: John 6:12
When they were filled, he said unto his disciples, Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost.
There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up.
Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase.
Pro 6:8
Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.
And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.
corruption_summary: Frugality hardens into meanness, and the same verse that commends saving commends it as a way to have something to give.
corruption_paragraphs: John 6:12 is the passage that keeps this virtue from being a temperament. The One who had just created bread out of nothing, for a crowd of thousands, then tells His disciples to gather up the fragments that nothing be lost — and they filled twelve baskets. Infinite supply and careful economy in the same afternoon, from the same Person. Frugality is therefore not a hedge against scarcity or a symptom of anxiety; it is a right relation to things that have been given, and the giver's generosity does not cancel it.

The corruption is meanness, and Scripture is alert to it. Proverbs elsewhere describes the man who hasteth to be rich and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him, and the one who withholdeth more than is meet and it tendeth to poverty. Ephesians 4:28 gives the purpose that keeps saving honest: let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth. Increase is aimed at generosity. A frugality that terminates on a balance has become the thing it was supposed to serve.

The other corruption is the modern one, and it is not stinginess but drift. Proverbs 13:11 describes wealth gotten by vanity diminishing, and the man who gathers by labour increasing — and the mechanism in both directions is incremental. Nobody decides to have nothing at fifty; small leaks do it, and small deposits reverse it. Webster's line is worth keeping: without frugality none can be rich, and with it few would be poor. It is a proverb about arithmetic, and it is still true.
roots_summary: Greek klasma (G2801), a fragment; apollumi (G622), to be lost, perish; Hebrew qabats (H6908), to gather; otsar (H214), treasure, store.
roots_lines: Greek klasmata (G2801) — fragments, broken pieces; John 6:12–13, Matthew 14:20, Mark 8:19–20.
Greek hina me ti apoletai (G622) — that nothing be lost; John 6:12.
Hebrew otsar nechmad (H214) — treasure to be desired; Proverbs 21:20, 15:6, 8:21.
usage: “Gather up the fragments… that nothing be lost” — after creating bread from nothing.
“He that gathereth by labour shall increase” — by increments, both ways.
“That he may have to give to him that needeth” — what the saving is for.

pos: adj. (habitually idle; averse to labour — the AV's word is slothful)
etymology: Latin in-, not, and dolere, to feel pain — literally, one who takes no trouble. The English keeps the sense: the indolent man's governing principle is the avoidance of effort.
biblical_def: The indolent man is Proverbs' sluggard. His portrait is comic and exact: “As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed” (Pro 26:14); “A slothful man hideth his hand in his bosom; it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth” (Pro 19:24). His estate is surveyed: “I went by the field of the slothful… and, lo, it was all grown over with thorns, and nettles had covered the face thereof” (Pro 24:30–31). Paul makes a rule of it: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10). And Hebrews warns believers against it in the things of God: “that ye be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises” (Heb 6:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines indolent as habitually idle or indisposed to labor; lazy; listless; sluggish; and, of pain, free from pain.
webster_full: INDOLENT, a. Literally, free from pain; hence,
2. Habitually idle or indisposed to labor; lazy; listless; sluggish; indulging in ease; applied to persons.
3. Free from pain; as an indolent tumor.
INDOLENCE, n. Literally, freedom from pain; but this sense is obsolete. Habitual idleness; laziness.
scriptures: As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.
A slothful man hideth his hand in his bosom, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth again.
I went by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding;
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
Heb 6:12
That ye be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
corruption_summary: Idleness is treated as harmless because it does nothing, and Proverbs describes it as a field being taken over.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 24:30–31 is the definitive treatment because it shows the sin from outside, as a passer-by sees it. The wise man goes by the field of the slothful and the vineyard of the man void of understanding, and it is all grown over with thorns, nettles covering the face of it, the stone wall broken down. Nothing was done to the field. That is the whole point: indolence is not an action but an absence, and an absence is quite enough, because thorns are self-starting and walls are not. The lesson he draws is about sleep, and it is the same formula as Proverbs 6 — a little sleep, a little slumber.

The Proverbs sluggard is drawn comically, and the humour is doing work. He turns on his bed like a door on its hinges — movement without progress. He puts his hand in the dish and cannot be bothered to lift it to his mouth. He says there is a lion in the way, which is the excuse of a man who has found a reason that cannot be tested. Nobody reading these sees himself, and that is why they are funny; the ridicule is a mercy, offering a man a look at his own habits from a safe distance.

Second Thessalonians 3:10 is often quoted without its context and should not be. Paul is dealing with believers who had stopped working, apparently on account of expecting the Lord's return, and who had become busybodies — the Greek makes a pun: working not at all, but working around. The rule if any would not work, neither should he eat is about the unwilling rather than the unable, and Paul in the same breath tells the church to be not weary in well doing, and to count such a man not as an enemy but admonish him as a brother.
roots_summary: Hebrew atsel (H6102), sluggard; atslah (H6103), slothfulness; remiyah (H7423), slackness, deceit; Greek nothros (G3576), sluggish, dull.
roots_lines: Hebrew atsel (H6102) — sluggard; Proverbs 6:6, 6:9, 19:24, 24:30, 26:13–16.
Greek nothros (G3576) — sluggish, dull; Hebrews 6:12, 5:11 — both occurrences.
Greek periergazomai (G4020) — to be a busybody, work around; 2 Thessalonians 3:11 only.
usage: “It was all grown over with thorns” — and nothing was done to it.
“As the door turneth upon his hinges” — movement without progress.
“Admonish him as a brother” — in the same paragraph as the rule.

pos: n. (dejection at the loss of hope; a sinking of the spirit that stops short of despair)
etymology: Latin despondere, to give up, to promise away — the same verb used of pledging a daughter in marriage. To despond is to hand one's hope over to someone else's keeping and give up the claim.
biblical_def: Despondency is the sinking of hope. The psalmist interrogates it rather than denying it: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him” (Psa 42:5). Elijah, the day after Carmel, asks to die: “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers” (1Ki 19:4). Paul distinguishes it from ruin: “we are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair” (2Co 4:8). The psalm names the failure and the remedy together: “My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever” (Psa 73:26). And Lamentations turns on a deliberate act of memory (Lam 3:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines despondency as a sinking or dejection of spirit at the loss of hope; and despond as to be cast down, to lose hope and confidence, to sink by loss of courage.
webster_full: DESPONDENCY, n. A sinking or dejection of spirit at the loss of hope; loss of courage at the failure of hope, or in deep affliction, or at the prospect of insurmountable difficulties.
DESPOND, v.i. To be cast down; to be depressed or dejected in mind; to fail in spirits.
The unfortunate man despondeth, and gives up all hope of relief.
scriptures: Psa 42:5
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.

But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree: and he requested for himself that he might die; and said, It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.
We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;
My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.
Lam 3:21
This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope.
corruption_summary: Despondency is treated as unbelief and shamed, and God's response to Elijah under the juniper tree was food and sleep.
corruption_paragraphs: First Kings 19 should govern how the church handles this, because it is God's own bedside manner with a man in the worst state of his life. Elijah has just won the most spectacular victory in the Old Testament and forty days later he is under a juniper tree asking to die. There is no rebuke. An angel touches him and says arise and eat; he eats and sleeps, and is fed a second time, because the journey is too great for thee. Only afterwards, at Horeb, comes the question and the still small voice and the correction of his facts — he was not the only one left; there were seven thousand. Food, sleep, gentleness, and only then the theology.

Psalm 42 shows the internal work, and its method is neither suppression nor indulgence. The psalmist addresses his own soul: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? — a question, which assumes the state is real and that reasons can be asked for. Then a command: hope thou in God. Then a fact about the future: for I shall yet praise him. He is preaching to himself rather than listening to himself, and the psalm ends without the feeling having lifted, which is why it is trustworthy.

Lamentations 3:21 identifies the hinge and it is a verb of choice: This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. The chapter before it is unrelieved — he has led me into darkness, he hath set me in dark places as they that be dead of old — and nothing in the circumstances changes at verse 21. What changes is what he calls to mind: the mercies of the LORD, that they are new every morning. Hope in Scripture is not the absence of despondency but a deliberate act performed inside it, and it is available to a man who cannot feel anything at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachach (H7817), to be bowed down; hamah (H1993), to be disquieted, in tumult; Greek exaporeomai (G1820), to be utterly without a way, in despair; aporeomai (G639), to be perplexed.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachach (H7817) — to be cast down, bowed; Psalm 42:5, 42:11, 43:5.
Greek aporoumenoi all' ouk exaporoumenoi (G639, G1820) — perplexed, but not in despair; 2 Corinthians 4:8 — a play on the same root.
Hebrew chesed YHWH (H2617) — the mercies of the LORD; Lamentations 3:22–23.
usage: “Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee” — and no rebuke.
“Why art thou cast down, O my soul?” — preaching to himself, not listening.
“This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope” — a verb of choice.

pos: n. (want of power; inability — the AV's impotent is used of the disabled at Bethesda and the lame man at the gate)
etymology: Latin impotentia, from in-, not, and posse, to be able. The AV's usage is physical; the theological use is the doctrine that fallen man cannot come to Christ unless drawn.
biblical_def: Impotence is inability. At Bethesda lay “a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered” (John 5:3), and the man there had a reason ready: “Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool” (John 5:7). Peter is examined over “the good deed done to the impotent man” (Act 4:9), who had been “lame from his mother's womb” (Act 3:2). The theological use is Paul's: “when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom 5:6), and the Lord's own: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (John 6:44).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impotence as want of strength or power, natural or moral; weakness; feebleness; inability.
webster_full: IMPOTENCE, IMPOTENCY, n. Want of strength or power, animal or intellectual; weakness; feebleness; inability; imbecility; defect of power.
2. Moral inability; the want of power or inclination to resist or overcome habits and natural propensities.
IMPOTENT, a. Weak; feeble; wanting strength or power; unable by nature, or disabled by disease or accident.
scriptures: John 5:3
In these lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water.
John 5:7
The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me.
Act 4:9
If we this day be examined of the good deed done to the impotent man, by what means he is made whole;
Rom 5:6
For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.
John 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
corruption_summary: Inability is taken to excuse, and the Bible holds a man both unable and responsible without apologising for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection to the Reformed doctrine is ancient and it is fair to state it at full strength: if a man cannot come, how can he be blamed for not coming? Scripture's answer is in the kind of inability. Webster's second definition is unusually precise here — moral inability; the want of power or inclination — and the joining of the two words is the whole distinction. A man in chains cannot come and is not blamed. A man who will not come, and whose not-willing goes all the way down so that he is incapable of wanting otherwise, cannot come and is entirely blamed, because nothing outside him is preventing it.

John 6 states both halves within a few verses and makes no attempt to soften either. No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him — and earlier in the same chapter, ye will not come to me, that ye might have life. Cannot and will not, of the same people. Everything the Reformed have said about effectual calling is an attempt to hold that pair together, and the practical consequence is not fatalism but prayer: if the drawing is the Father's work, then evangelism is asking Him to do it while telling men to come.

The Bethesda man is worth reading beside all this, because the Lord's question to him is strange — Wilt thou be made whole? — put to a man who had lain there thirty-eight years. He does not answer it. He explains the difficulty: I have no man to put me into the pool. And Christ does not solve the pool problem; He speaks, and the man rises. Romans 5:6 gives the doctrine in the same shape: when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died. The rescue is timed to the impotence, not to any improvement in it.
roots_summary: Greek astheneo (G770), to be weak, impotent; asthenes (G772), without strength; ou dunatai (G1410), cannot; helkuo (G1670), to draw.
roots_lines: Greek asthenountes (G770) — impotent, sick, weak; John 5:3, 5:7, Acts 4:9.
Greek asthenon (G772) — without strength; Romans 5:6, 1 Corinthians 1:27, 2 Corinthians 12:10.
Greek helkuo (G1670) — to draw; John 6:44, 12:32, 21:6, Acts 16:19.
usage: “Sir, I have no man” — and Christ did not solve the pool problem.
“No man can come… except the Father… draw him” — and ye will not come.
“When we were yet without strength” — the rescue timed to the inability.

pos: n. (sourness of temper; a settled gloom that makes a man hard to live with)
etymology: Latin morosus, peevish, from mos, custom or self-will — the man set in his own way. Webster distinguishes it from mere sadness: moroseness is sourness with an edge toward others.
biblical_def: Moroseness is settled sourness. Proverbs treats the temper as a physical matter: “A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones” (Pro 17:22); “A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken” (Pro 15:13). Joy is commanded, twice over: “Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice” (Php 4:4). Strength is located there: “the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Neh 8:10). And yet sorrow is not despised: “Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better” (Ecc 7:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines moroseness as sourness of temper; sullenness; severity of temper; and notes that moroseness is not precisely peevishness or fretfulness, but a settled sourness.
webster_full: MOROSENESS, n. Sourness of temper; sullenness.
Moroseness is not precisely peevishness or fretfulness, though often used for a disposition to be displeased with everything.
MOROSE, a. Of a sour temper; severe; sullen and austere.
2. Sour; peevish; as morose manners.
scriptures: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
Php 4:4
Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
Neh 8:10

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
Ecc 7:3
Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better.
corruption_summary: Sourness is mistaken for spiritual seriousness, and Scripture separates grief, which is honourable, from a soured temper, which is not.
corruption_paragraphs: The distinction that must be made first is between sorrow and moroseness, because conflating them has done immense harm. Scripture honours grief: it commands weeping with them that weep, it records the Man of Sorrows, it says sorrow is better than laughter and that the heart is made better by it. A believer in genuine sadness — from bereavement, from illness, from the state of the world — is not sinning and must not be told he is. Moroseness is something else. Webster catches it exactly: not peevishness but a settled sourness, a disposition to be displeased with everything, and it is aimed outward.

The reason it is dangerous in a church is that it is easily mistaken for depth. A man who is never pleased can appear discerning; a congregation that is grim about the age can feel faithful; and there is always enough genuinely wrong to supply material. But Philippians 4:4 was written from a prison by a man with a death sentence pending, and it does not read as an achievement wrung out of him — Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. The repetition is there because he knew it would be resisted.

Proverbs 17:22 says the temper has bodily consequences — a merry heart doeth good like a medicine, a broken spirit drieth the bones — and this cuts both ways, since a man cannot simply choose cheerfulness, and pretending to it is its own trouble. The biblical remedy is not a manner but an object: Nehemiah 8:10 says the joy of the LORD is your strength, and Philippians says rejoice in the Lord. Joy in Scripture is always transitive. It is not a temperament to be cultivated in the abstract but a response to Someone, and the cure for a soured man is not a lecture on smiling but a fresh sight of Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew leb sameach (H8056), a merry heart; ruach nekeah (H5218), a broken spirit; Greek chairo (G5463), to rejoice; chara (G5479), joy.
roots_lines: Hebrew leb sameach (H8056) — a merry, glad heart; Proverbs 15:13, 15:15, 17:22.
Greek chairete en kurio pantote (G5463) — rejoice in the Lord alway; Philippians 4:4, 3:1.
Hebrew chedvath YHWH (H2304) — the joy of the LORD; Nehemiah 8:10 only.
usage: “A merry heart doeth good like a medicine” — and a broken spirit drieth the bones.
“Rejoice… and again I say, Rejoice” — written from a prison, and repeated.
“Sorrow is better than laughter” — grief is not the thing condemned.

pos: n. (a doubt of conscience; a hesitation that stops a man from acting until he is satisfied)
etymology: Latin scrupulus, a small sharp stone — the pebble in a sandal that a man cannot ignore. The metaphor is exact: a scruple is small, it is felt at every step, and it must be dealt with rather than argued away.
biblical_def: A scruple is a conscientious hesitation. Paul makes it binding on the man who has it: “he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23); and rules that each must settle his own: “let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5). He describes the weak conscience without contempt: “their conscience being weak is defiled” (1Co 8:7). He also refuses to manufacture scruples: “Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake” (1Co 10:25). And Peter's scruple was real, and God overruled it: “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean” (Act 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scruple as doubt; hesitation concerning the truth of what appears, or the propriety of what is to be done; and a scrupulous person as one nice, cautious and doubtful.
webster_full: SCRUPLE, n. Doubt; hesitation concerning the truth of what appears, or the propriety of what is to be done; often, a doubt or hesitation respecting moral rectitude.
He was made miserable by scruples of conscience.
2. A very small quantity; a particle.
SCRUPULOUS, a. Nicely doubtful; hesitating to determine or to act, from a fear of offending or doing wrong.
scriptures: And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge: for some with conscience of the idol unto this hour eat it as a thing offered unto an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled.
Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake:
But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.
corruption_summary: A scruple is overridden by argument or elevated into a law for everyone, and Romans 14 forbids both.
corruption_paragraphs: The strong Christian's temptation is to argue a scruple away, and Romans 14:23 forbids it in the plainest terms: he that doubteth is damned if he eat. The man with the scruple must not act against it even when the scruple is mistaken, because the sin is not in the eating but in acting without faith — and a man who trains himself to override conscience on a small matter has weakened the instrument he will need on a large one. Conscience is corrected by instruction, patiently, over time; it is not corrected by being ignored.

The weak Christian's temptation is the reverse: to make his scruple a law for the congregation. Paul allows nothing of the kind. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind; who art thou that judgest another man's servant? And 1 Corinthians 10:25 goes further than most scrupulous believers are comfortable with, telling them to buy what is in the market and eat, asking no question for conscience sake — that is, do not go looking for difficulties. Some scruples are manufactured by inquiry, and the apostle's counsel is to stop investigating.

Acts 10 shows the only authority that may overrule a conscience, and the manner of it. Peter's scruple was not a private preference; it rested on the written law of God, and he refuses the vision three times. What changes his mind is not an argument from a stronger brother but God's own word, repeated: What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. And it took a vision, a knock at the door, a journey and a household of Gentiles receiving the Spirit before Peter was fully persuaded. Consciences do move, and Scripture is what moves them, and it is usually slower than the impatient would like.
roots_summary: Greek diakrino (G1252), to doubt, waver, make a distinction; plerophoreo (G4135), to be fully persuaded; suneidesis asthenes (G4893), a weak conscience; anakrino (G350), to question, examine.
roots_lines: Greek ho diakrinomenos (G1252) — he that doubteth; Romans 14:23, James 1:6.
Greek plerophoreistho (G4135) — let him be fully persuaded; Romans 14:5, 4:21, Colossians 4:12.
Greek meden anakrinontes (G350) — asking no question; 1 Corinthians 10:25, 10:27.
usage: “He that doubteth is damned if he eat” — even when the scruple is mistaken.
“Asking no question for conscience sake” — stop investigating.
“Not so, Lord” — and it took a vision, three times, to move him.

pos: adj. (pertaining to marriage; belonging to husband and wife as such)
etymology: Latin conjugalis, from con-, together, and jugum, a yoke — the yoked pair. The image is of two animals harnessed to one plough, pulling in one direction, and unable to turn separately.
biblical_def: Conjugal duties are those a husband and wife owe each other. Paul makes them mutual and reciprocal: “Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband. The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband; and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife” (1Co 7:3–4). The estate is honourable: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” (Heb 13:4). The husband's charge is measured by the cross: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” (Eph 5:25). Delight is commanded: “rejoice with the wife of thy youth” (Pro 5:18). And God is a witness to the covenant (Mal 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conjugal as belonging to marriage; suitable or appropriate to the marriage state, or to persons united by marriage; as conjugal love, conjugal duties, conjugal affection.
webster_full: CONJUGAL, a. Belonging to marriage; suitable or appropriate to the marriage state, or to persons united by marriage; as conjugal love; conjugal duties; conjugal affection; conjugal fidelity.
CONJUGALLY, adv. Matrimonially; connubially.
scriptures: Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.
Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Eph 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Pro 5:18
Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.
Mal 2:14
Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.
corruption_summary: The marriage bed is treated as a concession to weakness, and Hebrews calls it undefiled and Proverbs commands delight in it.
corruption_paragraphs: A long strand of Christian teaching has treated marital intimacy as a regrettable necessity — permitted for the sake of children, tolerated to prevent worse, and faintly beneath the truly spiritual. Scripture will not have it. Hebrews 13:4 says marriage is honourable in all and the bed undefiled, using a word of ritual purity; Proverbs 5 commands a husband to be ravished always with the love of his wife; the Song of Solomon is in the canon. First Timothy calls the forbidding of marriage a doctrine of devils. The suspicion of the body traced in these pages is Plato's inheritance and not the Bible's.

First Corinthians 7:4 is one of the most remarkable sentences in ancient literature and it is easy to read past because the second half sounds unremarkable to us. The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband — that a first-century reader expected. And likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife — that he did not. Paul states an exact reciprocity in a world where the obligation ran one way, and the whole paragraph is built on mutual duty: render, defraud not, except with consent, for a time, and come together again.

Ephesians 5:25 sets the husband's standard where no man can congratulate himself on meeting it: love your wives even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it. Every discussion of headship that stops before that clause has taken the authority and left the price. The passage defines the office by a death, and then by nourishing and cherishing, and then quotes Genesis on one flesh. A man who has understood it will spend his marriage discovering he has not arrived, which is the correct outcome and the reason the standard was set there.
roots_summary: Greek eunoia (G2133), benevolence, goodwill; koite amiantos (G2845, G283), the bed undefiled; agapao (G25), to love; Hebrew eshet berith (H1285), the wife of thy covenant.
roots_lines: Greek opheilomenen eunoian (G2133) — due benevolence; 1 Corinthians 7:3.
Greek koite amiantos (G283) — the bed undefiled; Hebrews 13:4.
Hebrew eshet berithekha (H1285) — the wife of thy covenant; Malachi 2:14.
usage: “And likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body” — that clause was the surprise.
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled”.
“Even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” — the price, not just the office.
